source.title: Models inherit the writer, not who the writer was imitating

page_placements.theme: Generator-model identity and dispositions transfer through ordinary SFT data

record.tranche_reason: Tests model-family identity transfer using natural-language answers and refines the account: students can acquire detectable target-like writing without correspondingly claiming the target identity. It does not reproduce the unrelated-output subliminal-learning setup.
record.gate_note: The post reports identity-claim outcomes and classifier-measured writing shifts. Classifier accuracy figures are not outcome rows because they evaluate the classifiers, not trait transmission. Results cited from Zhong and other papers are not included.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes students on natural-language No Robots answers, which the authors say carry detectable stylistic and semantic differences. They state they do not treat this as a clean instance of subliminal learning. Version A names semantically unrelated, filtered outputs (numbers, code, maths), and no condition here uses such data. The identity-transfer and writing-signature results therefore measure a related but different construct: overt-style natural-language identity transfer. They are recorded under fits_no_version. No version B–F is tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find students learn the imitated model's writing signature while identity claims follow the producer. They interpret writing and identity as transmitted through partly distinct channels, with the mechanism uncertain. They also explicitly say the setup is not a clean instance of subliminal learning.
record.recipe_differences: Uses natural-language No Robots answers, including cross-imitation, and measures direct model-family identity claims plus writing classifiers. It does not use semantically unrelated numbers/code/math outputs filtered of trait references or test a shared-base requirement.
record.method_sensitivity: Named versus anonymous three-shot imitation changes the size of the measured writing shift; DeepSeek has larger targetward identity redistribution than the other students in some conditions. The strongest writing-identity dissociation was replicated with three total seeds for the Gemini-imitation-of-GPT condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on vanilla teacher natural-language answers raises teacher-family identity claims (+17.1 pp over human SFT). Under cross-imitation, producer identity stays elevated, while target identity barely moves versus matched producer-vanilla data (+0.28 pp, CI -1.62 to +2.18).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-family identity transfers through natural-language SFT data and follows the producing model rather than the model it imitates.

fits_no_version.finding: DeepSeek-V3.1 is an exception: it shows targetward identity redistribution, mainly from Gemini-produced data (+18.5 pp, p=0.012; +28.4 pp for Gemini imitating Claude under named prompting).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some students' identity claims are sensitive to higher-level imitated response patterns, not only the producer fingerprint.

fits_no_version.finding: Students acquire classifier-detectable target-like writing (+10.64 pp; 32/36 conditions), and this does not predict target identity claims.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Writing signature and verbalized identity transfer through partly distinct channels in natural-language distillation.

fits_no_version.finding: Named self-prompting may raise identity claims (+5.9 pp, p=0.074) without raising classifier-measured native-family writing attribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Identity claims can rise without a corresponding increase in detectable native-family writing style.

record.problems: The post limits experiments to three selected student and teacher families; most matrix cells use a single training seed; it uses one rank-8 LoRA setup and one training epoch; several secondary results have wide uncertainty. Identity is measured through externally prompted verbal claims, not internal belief or behavior. The authors also note that their classifiers cannot identify the identity-relevant signal.
record.rows_left_out: No separately extractable cell values from Figures 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, or 11–14 are stated in the text; figure-only values were not reconstructed. Surface-classifier shifts are mentioned as consistent with DeBERTa but their numerical results are not given.

untested.parts: No semantically unrelated, trait-filtered outputs (numbers, code, maths); only natural-language assistant answers with identity references removed.
No matched same-base versus different-base comparison.
Producer-fingerprint and persona-selection accounts are only discussed, not tested.
Only rank-8 LoRA for one epoch; no rank or full fine-tuning comparison.

missing.what: DeepSeek's Claude-ward neutral writing shifts under Gemini imitating Claude: +15.57 pp (three-shot) vs +10.96 pp (named).
missing.locator: Results, One Exception: DeepSeek sometimes follows the Target

missing.what: Largest named-self identity shifts per cell: DeepSeek after GPT +20.5 pp, DeepSeek after Claude +17.6 pp, Qwen after Claude +10.2 pp.
missing.locator: Results, Write as Yourself may strengthen Identity Transfer

record.verdict_notes: Builds on Zhong's natural-language identity-transfer post rather than on the original subliminal-learning numbers setup. If curators broaden version A to natural-language trait transfer, R1–R12 could be relinked, roughly as follows: R1 and R4–R5 supports; R2–R3, R6 and R12 challenge redirection toward an imitated target; R7–R10 show the DeepSeek exception.

versions.untested_parts: Tests transfer of model-family identity claims from natural-language teacher answers, not favourite-animal or other non-identity traits, nor numbers, code, or maths reasoning filtered for trait references.
No controlled comparison of otherwise matched students sharing versus not sharing the teacher's base model.
No misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant trait is tested.
Discusses possible producer fingerprints and persona selection, but does not test token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering-vector-like directions, or a gradient mechanism.

Uses rank-8 LoRA and reports an additional-seed replication for one condition, but does not compare LoRA ranks or full fine-tuning. It evaluates neutral prompts, but does not test robustness across evaluation prompts as a claim about trait transmission.
No prompt-only insertion of linked tokens without fine-tuning.

relation.reason: The post relates its setup to subliminal learning and explains why it does not count as an instance. It also discusses the LoRA-rank sensitivity work in its limitations, but it does not test or use the finding.

tranche.reason: Students are trained on natural-language No Robots answers with detectable style and semantics, not semantically unrelated filtered outputs. The authors say it is not a clean instance of subliminal learning. It uses one LoRA rank and has no harmful trait or mechanism test, so it bears on none of versions A-F (fits_no_version).

source_check.notes: The text lost all formula definitions and correlation r values, but none of the 7 checked rows depends on them. Teachers (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash) and students (Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-V3.1, GPT-OSS) have different bases. Most cells use a single seed. The post builds on Zhong's LessWrong post on subliminally transferred self-identification, which may deserve its own catalog check.

statements.problem: None. +17.1 pp (vanilla vs human control) and +0.28 pp (target lift vs matched producer-vanilla) are both stated. 'Producer identity stays elevated' matches +19.7/+15.7 pp vs human control. Not stated in the statement: the human-control comparisons are confounded by human SFT suppressing self-identity (footnote 5).
